App.Tagline: Biological neural network simulator & teaching workstation
Coding.Compare.Tip: Advantages and drawbacks of the coding strategies, and where they occur in the brain.
Coding.Latency.Text: The time of the first spike after stimulus onset carries the information: strong stimulus → early spike. A single spike suffices, so it is very fast.
Coding.Phase.Text: The spike position relative to a background oscillation (here 8 Hz theta) encodes the value: strong input fires early in the cycle. Observed in hippocampal place cells.
Coding.Population.Text: The joint activity of many neurons tuned to different “preferred” stimuli encodes the value; the population vector (weighted average) recovers it. Fault-tolerant and precise.
Coding.Raster.Tip: Top to bottom: rate code (green), latency code (yellow, vertical lines mark stimulus onsets), phase code (pink, with the 8 Hz theta wave behind) and population code (blue, 12 neurons with different preferences).
Coding.Rate.Text: Information is in the firing rate: stronger stimulus → more spikes per unit time. Robust, but decoding needs time (averaging).
Coding.Schemes.Tip: Each code transmits the same value s but uses time and neurons differently.
Coding.Stimulus.Tip: The value to encode, from 0 (weak) to 1 (strong) – e.g. light intensity or a movement direction.
Coding.Sweep.Tip: The stimulus varies slowly and sinusoidally between 0 and 1 so every code can be watched changing continuously.
Coding.Table.Phase.Robust: good if the oscillation is stable
Coding.Table.Rate.Brain: motor neurons, muscle force; sensory intensity
Coding.Tuning.Tip: Gaussian tuning curves of the 12 population neurons (faint lines), their present response (bars), the true stimulus (yellow, s) and the decoded value (dashed red, ŝ).
Common.Defaults.Tip: Restores the biologically typical defaults (τm = 20 ms, E_L = −70 mV, V_th = −50 mV, V_reset = −65 mV, R_m = 100 MΩ, τref = 2 ms).
Common.Speed.Tip: Simulation speed relative to real time. 0.1× = ten-fold slow motion: 100 ms of biological time per real second, so individual spikes are easy to follow.
Common.Step01.Tip: A single 0.1 ms integration step (pauses the simulation). The Bio-Debugger prints every computation of the step.
Common.WhatsHappening.Tip: A live plain-language explanation of what the simulation is doing right now – computed from the current parameters and state.
Debug.Freeze.Tip: Pauses the simulation and performs exactly one integration step.
Debug.Input: Effect of the input current (electrode + noise)
Debug.Leak: Leak current (the membrane relaxes towards rest)
Debug.NoSpike: NO → no spike, the cell keeps integrating
Debug.NoStep: No integration step yet – start or step the simulation.
Debug.RefractoryCheck: The cell is in its {0} ms post-spike refractory period – it cannot fire
Debug.RefractoryFormula: Refractory period: Na⁺ channels are inactivated, the membrane stays at V_reset
Debug.Spike: YES → SPIKE! Action potential, v ← V_reset = {0} mV
Debug.SynapticFormula: I = I_syn {0} + I_ext {1} + I_noise {2} pA   ({3} spikes arrived in this step)
Debug.Title: Step-by-step Bio-Debugger
Debug.Title.Tip: The full computation of the latest 0.1 ms integration step with real numbers: leak → input → Euler integration → threshold check. Pause the simulation and step to see how the neuron “thinks”.
Gloss.Ablation.Def: An experimental technique in which a focused laser destroys selected cells to study their role in the network.
Gloss.Ablation.Why: It demonstrates the fault tolerance of biological networks: losing a few neurons rarely causes a collapse.
Gloss.ActionPotential.Def: An all-or-none electrical impulse of about 1 ms and ~100 mV that travels along the axon without attenuation. It is generated by voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels.
Gloss.ActionPotential.Why: The nervous system's “digital” signal: information lies in the timing and rate of spikes, not in their shape.
Gloss.Dale.Def: A neuron uses the same transmitter at all its output synapses, so it is either excitatory or inhibitory. The cortex has about 80% excitatory and 20% inhibitory cells.
Gloss.Dale.Why: The balance of excitation and inhibition keeps the network stable; disrupting it can lead to seizures.
Gloss.Euler.Def: The simplest numerical integration: v(t + dt) = v(t) + dt · dv/dt. With a small step (here 0.1 ms) it is an accurate approximation.
Gloss.Euler.Why: The Bio-Debugger shows exactly this step – revealing how a differential equation becomes a computer simulation.
Gloss.GanglionCell.Def: The output neuron of the retina; its axons form the optic nerve. It has a centre–surround receptive field: ON cells respond to a bright centre, OFF cells to a dark centre.
Gloss.GanglionCell.Why: The retina already compresses the image: signals from ~100 million photoreceptors travel on ~1 million fibres, mostly encoding contrast.
Gloss.Hebb.Def: Donald Hebb's postulate (1949): if cell A repeatedly takes part in firing cell B, their connection is strengthened. In short: “cells that fire together wire together”.
Gloss.Hebb.Why: The basic principle of associative learning and memory; STDP is its timing-sensitive, refined version.
Gloss.Homeostasis.Def: Regulatory mechanisms (e.g. synaptic scaling, adaptive thresholds) that keep neuronal activity within a desirable range.
Gloss.Homeostasis.Why: It prevents Hebbian learning from running away; the adaptive threshold on the Recognition page is an example.
Gloss.LatencyCoding.Def: Information is carried by the time from stimulus onset to the first spike.
Gloss.LatencyCoding.Why: Extremely fast: it explains how we recognise an image in ~100 ms when a neuron can fire only 1–2 spikes.
Gloss.LateralInhibition.Def: Neighbouring neurons inhibit each other, which amplifies differences.
Gloss.LateralInhibition.Why: It produces edge enhancement, contrast boosting and optical illusions (Mach bands, Hermann grid); it is also the basis of winner-take-all networks.
Gloss.Lif.Def: A simple neuron model: τm · dv/dt = −(v − E_L) + R_m · I. The membrane sums (integrates) current like a capacitor while leaking, fires on crossing threshold and is then reset.
Gloss.Lif.Why: Simple enough to simulate thousands of copies in real time, yet it keeps the neuron's most important properties – neuromorphic chips use it too.
Gloss.Ltd.Def: A lasting decrease in synaptic strength.
Gloss.Ltd.Why: Without it, weights would only grow and saturate; forgetting and fine-tuning are as important as strengthening.
Gloss.Ltp.Def: A lasting (hours to years) increase in synaptic strength, e.g. through insertion of AMPA receptors.
Gloss.Ltp.Why: The most important cellular mechanism of learning and memory, first described in the hippocampus.
Gloss.Mea.Def: A plate carrying many (60 to several thousand) tiny electrodes on which neurons can be cultured; the electrodes record spikes at many sites at once and can also stimulate.
Gloss.Mea.Why: It is the interface between computer and living network – the electrode and raster plot of the Network page are its digital counterpart.
Gloss.MembranePotential.Def: The electrical voltage between the inside and the outside of the cell, created by the unequal distribution of ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, Ca²⁺) and the membrane's ion channels.
Gloss.MembranePotential.Why: It is the neuron's “state variable”: the model equations describe how it evolves over time.
Gloss.Neuromorphic.Def: Hardware and software that mimic the organisation of the nervous system: spiking neurons, memory local to synapses, event-driven operation (e.g. Intel Loihi, SpiNNaker, IBM TrueNorth).
Gloss.Neuromorphic.Why: It can use orders of magnitude less energy than conventional processors, making it promising for edge devices, robotics and real-time sensing.
Gloss.Neuron.Def: The basic unit of the nervous system: dendrites receive inputs, the cell body sums them and the axon transmits the output as action potentials to other cells. The human brain contains about 86 billion.
Gloss.Neuron.Why: Every higher brain function – perception, memory, decision – arises from neurons working together.
Gloss.Organoid.Def: A few-millimetre, three-dimensional cluster of neural tissue grown in the lab from stem cells; it shows some developmental features of the brain and produces spontaneous electrical activity.
Gloss.Organoid.Why: “Organoid intelligence” research tries to use living neurons for computation; organoids are also important for disease modelling and drug discovery.
Gloss.PhaseCoding.Def: Spike timing relative to a background brain wave (e.g. 4–12 Hz theta) encodes information.
Gloss.PhaseCoding.Why: Hippocampal place cells encode the animal's position this way (phase precession).
Gloss.PhasePlane.Def: A plane showing the states of a dynamical system (here v and dv/dt). Trajectories, fixed points and limit cycles reveal the system's possible behaviours.
Gloss.PhasePlane.Why: It explains geometrically – without solving equations – why a cell rests or fires rhythmically.
Gloss.PopulationCoding.Def: The joint activity of many neurons with different preferences encodes a value; it can be decoded e.g. with the population vector.
Gloss.PopulationCoding.Why: Fault-tolerant and precise – the motor cortex encodes movement direction this way, which brain–computer interfaces exploit.
Gloss.Psp.Def: The small voltage change a synaptic current causes in the postsynaptic cell: excitatory (EPSP, depolarising) or inhibitory (IPSP, hyperpolarising).
Gloss.Psp.Why: A single EPSP is usually too small to fire the cell – many nearly simultaneous inputs must add up. The Network page's oscilloscope shows these small steps.
Gloss.Raster.Def: A chart in which each row is a neuron and each dot a spike over time.
Gloss.Raster.Why: It reveals the population pattern at a glance: asynchronous noise, synchronous stripes, rhythms or a group's response.
Gloss.RateCoding.Def: Information is carried by the number of spikes per unit time.
Gloss.RateCoding.Why: Robust and easy to measure, but slow; classical electrophysiology studied it most.
Gloss.ReceptiveField.Def: The part of the visual (or sensory) field a neuron responds to, and the pattern that drives it most strongly.
Gloss.ReceptiveField.Why: The hierarchy of receptive fields – dots, edges, shapes, objects – underlies vision and convolutional neural networks.
Gloss.Refractory.Def: The short period (1–3 ms) after a spike during which Na⁺ channels are inactivated and the cell cannot fire another action potential.
Gloss.Refractory.Why: It limits the maximum firing rate and ensures that spikes travel in only one direction along the axon.
Gloss.RestingPotential.Def: The membrane potential without input, typically −65 … −75 mV. It is maintained mainly by open K⁺ leak channels and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.
Gloss.RestingPotential.Why: It is the starting point: its distance from threshold sets how much input a spike requires.
Gloss.Rheobase.Def: The smallest constant current that – applied long enough – makes the cell fire. In the LIF model I_rh = (V_th − E_L) / R_m.
Gloss.Rheobase.Why: One of the key measures of excitability in experimental electrophysiology.
Gloss.Search.Tip: Search term names and definitions (in the current language).
Gloss.Seizure.Def: Pathological, excessively synchronous and strong neural activity, often caused by weakened inhibition or excessive excitation.
Gloss.Seizure.Why: You can replay it on the Experiments page: after inhibition is switched off, synchronous stripes appear on the raster plot.
Gloss.ShortTermDepression.Def: With frequent firing a synapse depletes its pool of releasable vesicles, so subsequent spikes are temporarily weaker (Tsodyks–Markram model, ~0.5 s recovery).
Gloss.ShortTermDepression.Why: A natural brake against runaway excitation: in the model it periodically interrupts the seizure-like bursts.
Gloss.SmallWorld.Def: A graph in which nodes connect mainly to their neighbours, yet a few random “shortcuts” keep the path between any two nodes short (Watts–Strogatz model).
Gloss.SmallWorld.Why: The brain's wiring is small-world: locally specialised yet globally integrated with short paths.
Gloss.Stdp.Def: A learning rule in which the change of a synapse depends on the time difference between pre- and postsynaptic spikes: pre first gives strengthening (LTP), post first weakening (LTD) – within a window of a few tens of milliseconds.
Gloss.Stdp.Why: It lets the network learn cause-and-effect relationships and temporal sequences without supervision.
Gloss.Synapse.Def: The junction between two neurons. A presynaptic spike releases neurotransmitter (e.g. glutamate, GABA) that triggers a current in the postsynaptic cell.
Gloss.Synapse.Why: The strength (weight) of synapses stores learned information – the brain's “memory” lives in its connections.
Gloss.Synchrony.Def: When many neurons fire at nearly the same time. The synchrony index (χ) measures it from 0 to 1: low values mean independent firing, high values coordinated firing.
Gloss.Synchrony.Why: Moderate synchrony (brain rhythms) aids communication; excessive synchrony is pathological, e.g. in epileptic seizures.
Gloss.Threshold.Def: The membrane potential (about −50 mV) at which an action potential is triggered.
Gloss.Threshold.Why: The threshold makes the neuron non-linear: small inputs are lost while sufficiently large ones trigger a spike – the basis of decision making.
Gloss.TimeConstant.Def: τm = R_m · C_m: the time in which a deviation of the membrane potential from rest decays to about 37%.
Gloss.TimeConstant.Why: It sets how long the cell “remembers” its inputs and how far apart spikes can be and still add up (temporal summation).
Gloss.V1.Def: The area of the occipital lobe where visual information first reaches the cortex. Its simple and complex cells are tuned to edges and bars of a given orientation (Hubel & Wiesel).
Gloss.V1.Why: Shape recognition starts here: higher-level visual representations are built from edges.
Gloss.Wetware.Def: Information processing carried out by living neural tissue. Neurons integrate inputs in an analogue way, communicate with discrete spikes and have their connections reshaped continuously by experience.
Gloss.Wetware.Why: The human brain runs on about 20 W yet outperforms supercomputers at many tasks. Understanding its principles promises new, energy-efficient computing.
Gloss.Wta.Def: A network motif in which strong mutual inhibition leaves only the most strongly driven neuron(s) active.
Gloss.Wta.Why: It implements decisions, categorisation and competitive learning – the Recognition network uses it to divide the digits among its neurons.

Home.Hero.Text: Biologically faithful neuron models, real-time spikes and learning synapses – all directly manipulable. Tune the parameters, watch the equations live and step through the computation millisecond by millisecond.
Home.Hero.Title: Discover how the living brain computes
Home.How.Text: Hover over any control, chart or variable to get an explanation. The “Guide” button at the top right shows suggested experiments for each page. The “What is happening now?” panels describe events live in plain language. Switch the language in the title bar at any time.
Home.How.Title: How to use it
Home.Model.Text: Leaky integrate-and-fire neurons (τm = 20 ms, E_L = −70 mV, V_th = −50 mV), 80% excitatory and 20% inhibitory cells, a Watts–Strogatz small-world graph, 1.5 ms synaptic delay, trace-based additive STDP, Tsodyks–Markram short-term depression and Poisson background noise. Integration: explicit Euler, dt = 0.1 ms.
Home.Model.Title: The model
Home.Modules.Sub: From a single cell through vision to pattern recognition.
Home.What.Text: “Wetware” is the computation performed by living neural tissue. Unlike silicon chips, neurons integrate in an analogue way, communicate with discrete spikes and constantly rewire their connections through experience. Neuromorphic engineers and brain-organoid researchers try to harness this principle for energy-efficient learning systems.

Net.AblatedCount.Tip: Number of neurons silenced by laser ablation.
Net.ClearAblations.Tip: Revive every neuron that was ablated.
Net.Controls.Tip: Electrode stimulation, plasticity and the balance of the network.
Net.Debugger.Note: The latest integration step of the selected neuron. Pause and step 0.1 ms at a time.
Net.DepressionRatio.Tip: If A−/A+ < 1 potentiation dominates and the weights drift up to w_max (saturation). If > 1 random firing causes net depression – which stabilises the network.
Net.Electrode.Tip: Inject current into the chosen neurons. Pick the targets with the “Stimulate” tool on the graph; if none are chosen the selected neuron receives the current.
Net.ElectrodeCurrent.Tip: Electrode current (0–500 pA). Above 200 pA even an isolated cell would fire continuously.
Net.Graph.Tip: 100 neurons on a ring: neighbouring links of the small-world graph are short arcs, random “shortcuts” long chords. Firing cells flash (like a calcium-imaging recording). Outgoing synapses of the selected neuron are coloured by weight; yellow dots are travelling action potentials.
Net.Heatmap.Tip: Row = presynaptic, column = postsynaptic neuron. Colour: synaptic weight on a blue (weak) → red/yellow (strong) scale; dark blue = inhibitory synapse, black = no connection. The band along the diagonal shows the ring's neighbour links.
Net.Histogram.Tip: Histogram of excitatory weights. Under additive STDP the distribution becomes bimodal over time: synapses end up either strong or weak.
Net.Inhibition.Tip: Multiplier on inhibitory (GABAergic) synapses. 0 = inhibition is lost: the network can become over-excited and start synchronous bursts (epileptiform activity).
Net.LearningRate.Tip: Multiplier on STDP weight changes. Larger values learn faster but noisier.
Net.MathLab.Tip: The selected neuron's equations with live values, real STDP events on the learning curve, the phase plane and the step-by-step Bio-Debugger.
Net.Metrics.Tip: Measures characterising the whole network, updated continuously.
Net.Narr.Ablate: Laser ablation: neuron {0} was destroyed. Its outgoing and incoming connections fell silent – watch how the network adapts.
Net.Narr.Desync: Synchrony has ended (χ = {0}): the network has returned to the asynchronous, healthy state.
Net.Narr.Electrode: Electrode: neuron {0} toggled, {1} cells now receive {2} pA.
Net.Narr.Fire: Neuron {0} fired: the sum of incoming synaptic current ({1} pA), external stimulation ({2} pA) and noise ({3} pA) pushed the membrane above threshold ({4} mV). About {5} input spikes arrived in the last ~30 ms.
Net.Narr.Loaded: Loaded: “{0}”. The network starts from a fresh initial state.
Net.Narr.Ltd: Because neuron {2} (post) fired {1} ms BEFORE neuron {0} (pre), the synaptic weight shrank by −{3} (LTD, non-causal coincidence) → w = {4}.
Net.Narr.Ltp: Because neuron {0} (pre) fired {1} ms before neuron {2} (post), the synaptic weight grew by +{3} (LTP, causal link) → w = {4}.
Net.Narr.Sync: Attention: the synchrony index is {0} – the network has started synchronous, seizure-like bursts! Vertical stripes have appeared on the raster plot.
Net.Narrator.Tip: Event log: why the selected neuron fired, which synapses strengthened or weakened and why, when the experiment changes phase and when the network synchronises.
Net.NoiseRate.Tip: Rate of Poisson events arriving from outside the network, per neuron. Without noise the network falls silent.
Net.Phase.Note: Trajectory of the selected neuron in the (v, dv/dt) plane. Synaptic inputs cause vertical jumps; the path breaks off at threshold and restarts after the reset.
Net.Phase.Tip: Current phase of the scenario and progress of the protocol.
Net.Plasticity.Tip: Turns spike-timing-dependent plasticity on/off. When off, the weights are frozen.
Net.Raster.Tip: Each row is a neuron (0–99), each dot a spike. Vertical stripes = synchronous bursts; scattered dots = asynchronous state. Click a row to select that neuron. The population firing rate is shown below.
Net.Rate.Tip: Average firing rate of living neurons over the last second. Cortical neurons typically fire at 1–10 Hz.
Net.Restart.Tip: Restart the current scenario from a fresh initial state.
Net.Scenario.Tip: Experimental scenario. Besides the free network you can load pre-configured teaching experiments.
Net.ScenarioControlled: These parameters are currently controlled by the running scenario.
Net.ScenarioInfo.Tip: Description of the current experiment: what it demonstrates and what to watch for.
Net.Scope.Tip: Membrane potential of the selected neuron (last 400 ms). Small EPSP steps, threshold crossings and resets are visible.
Net.Spikes.Tip: All action potentials fired since the start of the simulation.
Net.Step5.Tip: Advance 5 ms of simulated time (pauses the simulation).
Net.Strong.Tip: Percentage of plastic (excitatory) synapses stronger than half of w_max. STDP reshapes it continuously.
Net.Sync.Tip: Golomb–Rinzel synchrony index (χ): variance of the population-averaged activity relative to that of single cells. ≈ 0.1–0.2: asynchronous, healthy; > 0.4: strongly synchronous, seizure-like.
Net.Tool.Ablate.Tip: Virtually destroys the neuron (click again to restore it). Watch how the remaining network adapts.
Net.Tool.Select.Tip: Selects the clicked neuron: the oscilloscope, live equation and Bio-Debugger follow it.
Net.Tool.Stimulate.Tip: Adds (or removes) the clicked neuron to the electrode: the electrode current flows into these cells.
Net.Tool.Tip: What a click on the network graph does. Right click always selects.
Neuron.Amplitude.Tip: Strength of the injected current in picoamperes. 200 pA is the rheobase (default settings): below it the cell stays silent, above it fires rhythmically.
Neuron.Capacitance.Tip: C_m = τm / R_m: the charge-storing ability of the membrane. Larger cells (more membrane area) have a larger capacitance.
Neuron.Electrode.Tip: A virtual patch-clamp electrode injects current into the cell – exactly as in an electrophysiology lab.
Neuron.Equation.Hint: Tip: hover over the symbols – they highlight and show their biological meaning.
Neuron.Equation.Tip: The leaky integrate-and-fire equation with the current values under each variable. Hover over any symbol to see its biological meaning.
Neuron.Examples.Tip: Pre-set demos: load characteristic firing patterns with one click.
Neuron.FICurve.Note: The shape of this curve is the neuron's “transfer function”: the biological ancestor of activation functions in artificial neural networks.
Neuron.FICurve.Tip: Firing rate as a function of input current. It rises steeply at rheobase and saturates because of the refractory period. The red dot is the current operating point.
Neuron.FixedPoint.Tip: The voltage where dv/dt would be zero: v* = E_L + R_m · I. If v* is below threshold the membrane settles there; if above, it can never be reached and the cell fires repeatedly.
Neuron.Frequency.Tip: Frequency of the pulse train or sine wave.
Neuron.Measured.Tip: Spikes actually fired per second over the last 1 s of simulated time.
Neuron.Membrane.Tip: The biophysical constants of the LIF equation. Change them and watch the oscilloscope, phase plane and f–I curve transform.
Neuron.Narr.Above: The current ({0} pA) exceeds rheobase ({1} pA). The membrane heads towards v* = {2} mV, which is above threshold ({3} mV), so the cell fires rhythmically at about {4} Hz in theory: it charges, fires, resets and charges again.
Neuron.Narr.Below: The injected current ({0} pA) is below rheobase ({1} pA). The membrane settles at v* = {2} mV, below threshold ({3} mV) – so there is no firing. Raise the amplitude above rheobase!
Neuron.Narr.Noise: Noise makes firing irregular, and near threshold random spikes appear.
Neuron.Narr.Refractory: The cell has just fired and is in its {0} ms refractory period: Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so no stimulus can trigger another spike right now.
Neuron.Noise.Tip: Random current fluctuations (an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process) modelling the synaptic noise real neurons receive. With noise the cell can fire even below rheobase – “stochastic resonance”.
Neuron.Phase.Cycle: The fixed point v* = {0} mV lies above threshold ({1} mV), so the membrane never reaches it: it crosses threshold first, fires and jumps back to {2} mV. This “charge → fire → reset” loop is the limit-cycle-like behaviour of the LIF model (tonic firing).
Neuron.Phase.Stable: The fixed point v* = {0} mV lies below threshold: a stable equilibrium. After any small perturbation the membrane returns exponentially with a time constant of about {1} ms – the cell stays silent.
Neuron.PhasePlane.Tip: The classic view of dynamical systems. The line is dv/dt(v) for the present current; where it crosses zero lies the fixed point. The yellow dot and trail show the cell's current state.
Neuron.PulseWidth.Tip: Length of one current pulse. With short pulses the membrane has no time to charge to threshold – an effect of the leak (τm).
Neuron.ResetRule: v ≥ V_th  ⇒  spike;  v ← V_reset;  pause τ_ref
Neuron.Rheobase.Tip: The smallest constant current that eventually produces a spike: I_rh = (V_th − E_L) / R_m.
Neuron.Scope.Tip: The membrane voltage over time (top) and the injected current (bottom). The dashed red line is the threshold, the dotted green one the resting potential. Spikes appear as vertical peaks.
Neuron.Theory.Tip: For a constant current the LIF rate has a closed form: f = 1 / (τref + τm · ln((RI − (V_reset − E_L)) / (RI − (V_th − E_L)))). Without noise the measured rate matches it.
Page.Coding.Guide:
Move the stimulus slider and watch all four bands at once.
Rate coding produces more spikes – but needs time to average.
Latency coding answers with the very first spike: strong stimulus = early spike.
In phase coding the spike shifts relative to the theta wave.
Turn on the automatic sweep and compare the decoded value with the true one.
Page.Coding.Simple: The brain can only send clicks, but there are many ways to carry information with them. Imagine passing on the brightness of a lamp by knocking: (1) the brighter the light, the faster you knock (green band); (2) the SOONER you knock once after it is switched on (yellow); (3) you knock earlier or later relative to a background beat (pink, like syncopation in music); (4) many friends knock at once, each “specialised” in a different brightness, and who knocks loudest reveals the value (blue). Move the stimulus slider and watch all four patterns change together!

Start with the Neuron lab to understand a single cell.
Then open the Network page where 100 neurons work together.
The Experiments page launches ready-made demos with one click.
Hover over anything to get an explanatory tooltip.
Page.Home.Simple: Your brain consists of about 86 billion tiny cells (neurons) that talk to each other with minute electrical “clicks” – we call them spikes. A single cell is simple: it collects incoming signals and, once enough have piled up, it clicks too. The magic comes from huge numbers of these cells being connected, and from those connections growing stronger or weaker with experience – that is learning. This program makes all of it visible, from a single cell to a learning network. You need no biology background: every page starts with a yellow box like this one, explained in everyday terms.

Page.Network.Guide:
Click a neuron in the graph: the oscilloscope and the equation follow it.
Pick the “Stimulate” tool, select a few neurons and watch them fire.
Drop inhibition to 0 and raise excitation – synchronous bursts appear.
The “Laser ablation” tool silences neurons.
The scenario drop-down contains ready-made experiments (e.g. Pavlovian learning).
Page.Network.Simple: Here 100 “bucket cells” are connected like a group of friends where everyone passes news to a few neighbours and a few distant acquaintances. 80% of the cells are “encouragers” (excitatory, red): when one clicks it urges its neighbours to click too. 20% are “calmers” (inhibitory, blue): they quieten the others so the excitement does not run away. In the dotted chart on the left each row is a cell and each dot a click. In a calm state the dots are scattered; if you remove the calming, everybody starts shouting at once – vertical stripes appear, similar to what happens in an epileptic seizure.

Page.Neuron.Guide:
Pick the “Silent” example: the current is below rheobase, the cell stays quiet.
Drag the amplitude above 200 pA – action potentials appear.
Increase τm: the membrane charges more slowly and the rate drops.
Pause and step 0.1 ms at a time – the Bio-Debugger prints every computation.
Hover over the variables of the equation to see what they mean biologically.
Page.Neuron.Simple: Imagine a bucket filled from a tap (the input current) with a small hole in the bottom through which water keeps leaking (the “leak”). When the water reaches the rim (the threshold), the bucket tips over in an instant – that is a spike – and then starts filling again. If the tap runs only gently, the water leaks out as fast as it comes in and never reaches the rim: the cell stays silent. With a stronger tap it fills quickly and tips often: the cell fires frequently. On the chart the wavy line is the water level and the vertical spikes are the tip-overs. Drag the “Amplitude” slider and watch when the bucket starts tipping over!

Page.Recognition.Guide:
Press “+300 samples” or start training and watch the receptive fields turn into digits.
Pick a digit, add noise, then press Recognise.
Draw your own digit on the grid (right click = eraser).
The raster shows input pixels firing and a single output neuron winning.
Page.Recognition.Simple: Here 20 cells compete with each other, like a class where everyone wants to answer. We show them a digit (the pixels turn into clicks), and the cell that “recognises” it fastest wins. The winner adapts a little more to what it saw, while the others stay silent. So that the same cell does not win every time, each winner gets a little “tired” after a victory. Nobody tells them which digit is which – yet after a few hundred examples each cell specialises in one digit: you can see this in the small pictures at the bottom right. Press “+300 samples”, then “Recognise”!

Page.Scenarios.Guide:
Read what to watch for, then start the experiment.
On the network page the toolbar shows the current phase and progress.
The “What is happening now?” log explains every important event.
Page.Scenarios.Simple: These are pre-built “mini experiments” you can start with one click. Each one shows an interesting phenomenon: how the brain learns to link two things (Pavlov's dog), what happens when the calming cells fail (a seizure), what happens when learning is too eager (every connection maxes out), and how cells “encode” information. Once started, the program walks you through the stages by itself, and the “What is happening now?” panel tells you in plain words what you are seeing.

Page.Stdp.Guide:
Run the “Causal (pre → post)” example: the weight grows step by step (LTP).
Switch to the “Reversed” order: the weight shrinks (LTD).
Set Δt = 45 ms: the effect almost vanishes because the window is exponential.
With random timing the net drift is decided by the A+τ+ − A−τ− balance.
Page.Stdp.Simple: Think of Pavlov's dog: if the bell ALWAYS rings just before the food arrives, the dog learns that the bell means food. Connections between cells learn the same way: if cell “A” regularly clicks just BEFORE cell “B”, A probably helped make B click – so the A→B connection grows stronger (the circle on the right grows). If it is the other way round and B clicks first, A cannot have been the cause, so the connection weakens (the circle shrinks). The closer the two clicks are in time, the bigger the effect. Press the “Causal” or “Reversed” button and watch which way the circle changes!
Page.Stdp.SimpleTitle: In plain words: “cells that fire together wire together”
Page.Stdp.Subtitle: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity: how a synapse learns from timing
Page.Stdp.Tip: An interactive version of the Bi & Poo pairing protocol.

Page.Vision.Guide:
Look at the Hermann grid: ON-cell responses are weaker at the intersections – that is why we see grey dots there.
Pick Mach bands and click an image: the profile shows the overshoot at each step.
Switch off lateral inhibition – the illusions and the edge enhancement disappear.
Rotate the grating: the colour of the V1 orientation map follows the angle.
Draw your own picture or load a photo.
Page.Vision.Simple: Your eye does not work like a camera that sends every pixel. Retinal cells signal when a spot is BRIGHTER or DARKER than its immediate surroundings – so they send mostly edges and borders to the brain, like a sketch (panels 2–4). That is why you see grey dots at the crossings of the white grid although nothing is there: the cells keep comparing themselves with their neighbours, and that fools them. The cortex (panel 5) then works out which way these lines are tilted – the colours show the direction. Panel 6 shows how the image travels along the optic nerve as spikes.

Param.AMinus.Tip: LTD (depression) amplitude: how much the weight shrinks when the postsynaptic cell fires first.
Param.APlus.Tip: LTP (potentiation) amplitude: how much the weight grows when the presynaptic spike immediately precedes the postsynaptic one.
Param.EL.Tip: The voltage the membrane settles to without input. It is set mainly by K⁺ leak channels; typically −65 … −75 mV.
Param.Rm.Tip: Sets how much voltage a given current produces (Ohm's law: ΔV = R_m · I). High-resistance cells (small, or with few open channels) are more sensitive: a smaller current makes them fire.
Param.TauM.Tip: τm = R_m · C_m: the product of membrane resistance and capacitance. It sets how quickly the cell “forgets”: with a large τm inputs add up for longer (longer memory), with a small τm the membrane relaxes quickly to rest. Typical cortical value: 10–30 ms.
Param.TauMinus.Tip: Time constant of the LTD window. If τ− > τ+ the negative lobe is wider, causing net depression for random firing.
Param.TauPlus.Tip: Time constant of the LTP window: how far apart two spikes can be and still count as “causal”. Biologically set by NMDA receptor and Ca²⁺ dynamics (~15–20 ms).
Param.TauRef.Tip: The time after a spike during which Na⁺ channels are inactivated and the cell cannot fire again. It caps the firing rate (f_max ≈ 1/τref).
Param.VReset.Tip: After a spike the membrane is reset to this voltage (after-hyperpolarisation). The deeper it is, the longer it takes to reach threshold again – lowering the firing rate.
Param.VTh.Tip: When the membrane potential reaches this value, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open in an avalanche and an action potential (spike) is fired. The LIF model replaces this with a single threshold rule.
Preset.Fast.Tip: 480 pA: high rate, the refractory period becomes noticeably limiting.
Preset.Leaky.Tip: Short τm (8 ms) with short pulses: the membrane forgets quickly and summation is harder.
Preset.Noise.Tip: 170 pA + noise: the mean current is below rheobase, yet the noise triggers random spikes.
Preset.Pulses.Tip: 8 Hz, 30 ms current pulses: each pulse triggers a short burst of spikes.
Preset.Silent.Tip: 150 pA: below rheobase – the membrane stops at −55 mV, no spikes.
Preset.Tonic.Tip: 260 pA: regular rhythmic firing at about 37 Hz.
Rec.Accuracy.Tip: Hit rate on noisy test samples (measured every 100 training samples). Random guessing would score 10%.
Rec.AddNoise.Tip: Flips random pixels on the pad.
Rec.Boost: Too few output spikes – boosting the input ({0} Hz) and presenting again.
Rec.Digit.Tip: Load this digit's template onto the pad.
Rec.Field.Tip: Receptive field of output neuron {0}: bright = strong synapse.
Rec.Fields.Tip: The input weights of the 20 output neurons as 7×9 images. During training, prototypes of digits gradually emerge from random noise – this is what the network has learned.
Rec.How.1: Encoding: every pixel is an input neuron sending Poisson spikes according to brightness (60 Hz or 1 Hz).
Rec.How.2: Integration: the 20 output LIF neurons sum the weighted input spikes; the first to reach threshold fires.
Rec.How.3: Competition: the winner suppresses the others through lateral inhibition (winner-take-all), like the cortex's inhibitory interneurons.
Rec.How.4: Learning: STDP strengthens the winner's inputs that fired just before it and weakens the rest; the weights are normalised.
Rec.How.5: Homeostasis: each win raises the neuron's threshold slightly, giving other neurons a chance – this is how the network divides the digits among them.
Rec.LabelsInfo: {0}/{1} neurons have a label, covering {2} different digits.
Rec.Outputs.Note: Nobody taught these labels: the neurons specialised on their own; we only checked afterwards which digit each responds to.
Rec.Outputs.Tip: Spike counts of the 20 output neurons during the last presentation, with their assigned digit labels below.
Rec.Pad.Hint: Left mouse button: draw · right mouse button: erase
Rec.Pad.Tip: Each square is an input neuron. Bright pixels fire at 60 Hz, dark ones at 1 Hz (Poisson encoding).
Rec.Presentation.Tip: Top: spikes of the 63 input pixels (yellow); bottom: the 20 output neurons (purple). Thanks to lateral inhibition the winning neuron's spikes suppress the others.
Rec.Presenting: Presenting: the pixels send spikes and the output neurons compete…
Rec.QuickTrain.Tip: Present 300 training samples instantly (a fraction of a second).
Rec.Recognize.Tip: Presents the pad's pattern to the network as spikes for 150 ms and animates which output neuron wins.
Rec.ResetNet.Tip: An untrained network with random weights.
Rec.Result: Recognised digit: {0} (confidence {1}%). The winner was output neuron {2}; {3} output spikes in total.
Rec.ResultTitle.Tip: The recognised digit: the label whose neurons produced the highest average spike count.
Rec.Samples.Tip: Number of training samples presented so far.
Rec.Speed.Tip: How many training samples to present per frame.
Rec.TestNoise.Tip: The probability with which “Add noise” and the accuracy test flip each pixel. The network still recognises noisy patterns – just like biological vision.
Rec.TrainNoise.Tip: Pixel flip probability of the training samples. A little noise helps generalisation.
Rec.Training.Tip: The network sees noisy digits without labels. STDP pulls the winning neuron's input weights towards the pattern it saw, while adaptive thresholds make sure every neuron gets its turn.
Rec.Unknown: The network could not decide – it may not be trained yet, or the pattern differs strongly from what it learned.
Rec.Untrained: The network is still untrained: start training or press “+300 samples”!
Scenario.Coding.Observe: The green group (0–11) receives DC currents of increasing strength: the stronger the input, the denser the spikes (rate code). The pink group (50–61) receives the same bias on top of an 8 Hz theta rhythm: cells with stronger input fire earlier in the cycle (phase code) – diagonal stripes appear on the raster plot.
Scenario.Coding.Steps: Continuous: compare the patterns of the two coloured groups on the raster plot. For a detailed comparison open the Neural coding page.
Scenario.Coding.Title: Information coding modes
Scenario.Free.Observe: With balanced excitation and inhibition the neurons fire irregularly at low rates (≈ 4–6 Hz), as in the awake cortex. The synchrony index is low. Experiment freely with the controls!
Scenario.Free.Steps: No scripted protocol: use the electrode, the inhibition/excitation sliders or laser ablation.
Scenario.Free.Title: Free network
Scenario.Homeostasis.Observe: If depression (A−) is too weak compared with potentiation (A+) in the STDP rule, synapses run up towards w_max: the histogram shifts right, “Strong synapses” rise above 90% and the network loses selectivity. After the balance is restored the weights spread out again.
Scenario.Homeostasis.Phase.Imbalance: Imbalance: A− = 0.4 · A+. Random spike pairs strengthen synapses on average, so the weights keep growing. Watch the histogram and the “Strong synapses” meter!
Scenario.Homeostasis.Phase.Rebalanced: Balance restored: A− = 1.35 · A+. Random coincidences now cause net depression; only truly causal links stay strong. This is the essence of homeostatic regulation.
Scenario.Homeostasis.Steps:
0–20 s: A− = 0.4 · A+ – the weights saturate.
From 20 s: A− = 1.35 · A+ – depression dominates and the distribution recovers.
Scenario.Homeostasis.Title: Synaptic scaling & homeostasis
Scenario.Pavlov.Observe: Stimulation of group A (yellow, the “bell”) is regularly followed 8 ms later by stimulation of group B (purple, the “food”). The A→B weights grow before your eyes on the heatmap (dashed box), until in the test phase A alone makes B fire.
Scenario.Pavlov.Phase.Baseline: Baseline: only group A (the “bell”) is stimulated. Notice that group B does not respond – there is no association yet.
Scenario.Pavlov.Phase.Test: Test: only A is stimulated again – and now B fires on its own! The strengthened synapses deliver enough current. This is a cellular model of classical conditioning.
Scenario.Pavlov.Phase.Training: Training: stimulation of A is always followed 8 ms later by B. Because A's spikes causally precede B's spikes, STDP strengthens the A→B synapses (LTP). Watch the highlighted block of the heatmap!
Scenario.Pavlov.Steps:
0–3 s: only A is stimulated – B does not respond.
3–21 s: A is always followed by B (pairing) – STDP potentiates the A→B links.
From 21 s: only A is stimulated again – yet B fires: the network has learned the association.
Scenario.Pavlov.Title: Classical conditioning (Pavlovian Hebbian learning)
Scenario.Seizure.Observe: When inhibition is switched off and excitation is boosted, the disordered activity suddenly turns into massive synchronised population bursts: vertical stripes appear on the raster plot and the synchrony index jumps.
Scenario.Seizure.Phase.Normal: Normal operation: excitation and inhibition are balanced; neurons fire irregularly and independently.
Scenario.Seizure.Phase.Recovery: Recovery: inhibition is back, the synchronous bursts stop and the network returns to the asynchronous state. This is why antiepileptic drugs that boost GABAergic inhibition work.
Scenario.Seizure.Phase.Seizure: Seizure: inhibitory synapses are switched off and excitation is boosted. Recurrent excitation spreads like an avalanche and cells fire in synchronous volleys – depletion of synaptic resources interrupts the bursts periodically.
Scenario.Seizure.Steps:
0–4 s: normal, balanced network.
4–12 s: inhibition = 0, excitation × 4 – seizure.
From 12 s: inhibition returns – the network recovers.
Scenario.Seizure.Title: Synchronisation & seizure (epileptiform activity)
Scenarios.Start.Tip: Loads the scenario into the network simulator and opens it.
Shell.Guide.Tip: Step-by-step suggested experiments for the current page.
Shell.Language.Tip: Interface language. Switching applies instantly to every label, tooltip and explanation – no restart needed.
Shell.ModelInfo:
LIF neurons · STDP learning
Euler integration, dt = 0.1 ms
100 neurons · small-world network
Shell.ModelInfo.Tip: The built-in engine runs in C# with the same equations as the Brian 2 model of the specification: leaky integrate-and-fire membrane, trace-based STDP, Poisson background noise and short-term synaptic depression.
Shell.Simple.Tip: A jargon-free explanation built on everyday analogies at the top of the page – for newcomers and non-specialists.
Stdp.Animation.Tip: Top: presynaptic spike, bottom: postsynaptic spike. The dashed arrow is Δt; on the right the synaptic bouton whose size follows the weight.
Stdp.Balance.Negative: Negative balance: with random firing the synapse weakens on average – only genuine causal links survive. This gives stable, selective learning.
Stdp.Balance.Positive: Positive balance: even random firing strengthens the synapse – weights eventually saturate (see the homeostasis experiment).
Stdp.Balance.Tip: The area under the window. It decides what happens to the synapse when the two cells fire independently at random.
Stdp.Balance.Zero: Balanced window: with random firing the weight does not change on average.
Stdp.Biology.Text: The key is the NMDA receptor, a “coincidence detector”: it admits Ca²⁺ only when presynaptic glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation (the back-propagating action potential) are present together. A large, fast Ca²⁺ influx triggers insertion of AMPA receptors (LTP), a smaller, prolonged influx their removal (LTD). This is how a synapse learns from cause-and-effect timing.
Stdp.DeltaT.Tip: Positive Δt: the presynaptic spike comes first (causal order, potentiation). Negative Δt: the postsynaptic cell fires first (depression).
Stdp.Examples.Tip: Classic pairing experiments with one click.
Stdp.Explain.Ltd: Because the post-neuron fired {0} ms before the pre-neuron, this input cannot have caused the output: the weight shrank by −{1} (LTD point). New weight: {2}.
Stdp.Explain.Ltp: Because the pre-neuron fired {0} ms BEFORE the post-neuron, the input may have contributed to the output: the weight grew by +{1} (LTP point). New weight: {2}.
Stdp.Explain.Start: Start a pairing! I will show how and why the timing of the two spikes changes the strength of the synapse.
Stdp.Hebb.Quote: “When an axon of cell A is near enough to excite a cell B and repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing it, … A's efficiency, as one of the cells firing B, is increased.”
Stdp.Jitter.Tip: Biological imprecision: every pairing's Δt varies slightly at random.
Stdp.PairOnce.Tip: Trigger a single pre/post spike pair and show the weight change.
Stdp.Pairings.Tip: Number of pre/post spike pairs delivered so far.
Stdp.Preset.AntiCausal.Tip: The postsynaptic cell fires first: the input cannot have caused the output → LTD.
Stdp.Preset.Causal.Tip: The presynaptic cell fires 8 ms before the postsynaptic one: the input may have “caused” the output → LTP.
Stdp.Preset.Distant.Tip: Large time difference: the exponential window makes the change negligible.
Stdp.Preset.Random.Tip: Δt is random between −50 and +50 ms – as for two independent cells. The net direction is decided by the areas of the two lobes.
Stdp.Protocol.Tip: Modelled on the slice experiment of Bi & Poo (1998): the pre- and postsynaptic cells are stimulated repeatedly with a fixed delay while the synaptic strength is measured.
Stdp.Random.Tip: Δt is uniformly distributed in −50 … +50 ms.
Stdp.Rate.Tip: How many pairings per second the animation runs.
Stdp.Rule.Tip: The four parameters that shape the asymmetric, two-sided exponential STDP window.
Stdp.WeightHistory.Tip: The weight as a function of the number of pairings, bounded between 0 and w_max = 1.
Stdp.Window.Tip: Weight change versus time difference. Green: LTP (pre first), yellow: LTD (post first). Blue dots are completed pairings, the large dot is the latest one.
Stim.Constant.Tip: A continuous, unchanging current – the classic step-current experiment.
Stim.Noisy.Tip: A strongly fluctuating current mimicking real synaptic bombardment.
Stim.Pulses.Tip: Repeating square pulses. Short pulses reveal the integrating and leaking behaviour of the membrane.
Stim.Ramp.Tip: A linearly increasing current: see at which current firing starts (rheobase) and how it accelerates.
Stim.Sine.Tip: A sinusoidal current: the cell fires on the peaks of the wave (phase locking).
Stim.Step.Tip: A current switching off and on every half period: shows charging and relaxation.
Term.DvDt: dv/dt – the rate of change of the membrane potential (mV/ms). Positive means depolarisation (moving towards threshold), negative means repolarisation. It is the vertical axis of the phase plane.
Term.EL: E_L – leak (resting) potential. The −(v − E_L) term pulls the membrane back towards this value like a spring: this is the “leaky” part of the model.
Term.I: I – the current injected through the electrode (pA). Positive current depolarises. A constant current above rheobase produces rhythmic firing.
Term.Iext: I_ext – external stimulation: current injected by the electrode or by the experimental scenario.
Term.Inoise: I_noise – Poisson background noise: models the random bombardment from thousands of synapses outside the network. It makes firing irregular and lifelike.
Term.Isyn: I_syn – the sum of incoming synaptic currents. Excitatory synapses give positive (EPSC), inhibitory synapses negative (IPSC) currents decaying with a 5 ms time constant. The weight (w) scales the amplitude.
Term.Rm: R_m – membrane resistance. Converts current into voltage according to Ohm's law (R_m · I). With 100 MΩ, 200 pA produces exactly 20 mV of depolarisation – precisely the gap between rest and threshold.
Term.TauM: τm – membrane time constant. Biologically the product of membrane capacitance (C_m, the lipid bilayer) and resistance (R_m, the ion channels). It sets the length of the cell's “memory”: the time for a voltage deviation to decay to about 37%.
Term.V: v – the membrane potential: the voltage between the inside and outside of the cell. The colour shows the state: green = near rest, yellow = depolarised, red = near threshold / spike.
Vision.Angle.Tip: Tilt of the bar or grating. Watch the V1 orientation map change colour.
Vision.Center.Tip: Radius of the excitatory centre of the receptive field. Larger values give a blurrier image, sensitive to coarser detail.
Vision.Clear.Tip: A dark blank input for your own drawing.
Vision.Explain.Bars: An oriented bar: centre–surround cells only signal its edges, but V1 cells also signal its orientation. Rotate it with the angle slider and watch the colour of the V1 map change – this is how the cortex “sees” edge direction.
Vision.Explain.Checkerboard: Corners and edges of the checkerboard drive strong ON/OFF responses, the uniform interiors almost none. The V1 map shows horizontal and vertical edges in different colours.
Vision.Explain.Custom: Your own input: notice how the retina suppresses uniform areas and forwards only edges, while V1 also encodes the orientation of those edges.
Vision.Explain.Disc: A bright ring: the inner and outer borders have opposite contrast, so ON and OFF cells respond at swapped positions. The V1 map shows every orientation around the circle – a rainbow ring.
Vision.Explain.Face: A simple face. After the retina only the contours remain – a line drawing. Actual face recognition happens much later, in the face area of the inferior temporal lobe, but the edges it needs are extracted right here.
Vision.Explain.Gradient: The two inner squares are exactly the same grey (0.5), yet the one on the dark background looks lighter and the one on the light background darker. Ganglion cells signal contrast relative to the surround, not absolute brightness. Hover over the squares: I = 0.50 on both!
Vision.Explain.Grating: A sine grating – the basic stimulus of vision research. Matching the λ slider to the grating period (12 px) maximises the V1 response: the cells are tuned to spatial frequency as well.
Vision.Explain.HermannGrid: We see grey dots at the intersections of the white streets although they are just as white. Reason: an ON cell at an intersection receives light in its surround from four directions (strong inhibition), but only from two in the middle of a street. Look at panel 2: the response really is weaker at the intersections!
Vision.Explain.MachBands: Each band is a uniform grey, yet we see lighter/darker stripes at the borders. Lateral inhibition amplifies boundaries: an overshoot on the bright side and an undershoot on the dark side. Click the image and look at the intensity profile!
Vision.Explain.Mondrian: Overlapping rectangles. Centre–surround filtering transmits local contrast instead of absolute brightness – which is why colours and greys look stable under changing illumination (colour constancy).
Vision.Explain.NoisySquare: A noisy image hiding a square. Averaging over the centre (σc) reduces noise while surround inhibition highlights the square's edges. Increase σc: the noise disappears but the edges blur too – the trade-off between resolution and noise robustness.
Vision.Explain.Tip: What explains what you see in the chosen stimulus?
Vision.Inhibition.Tip: Strength of the surround relative to the centre. 1 = full balance: no response to uniform light, only to contrast. 0 = no inhibition: the cell simply follows brightness.
Vision.Kernel.DoG.Tip: Difference of Gaussians (DoG): excitatory centre, inhibitory ring – the receptive field of an ON-centre ganglion cell.
Vision.Kernel.Gabor.Tip: Gabor filter: the receptive field of a V1 simple cell, sensitive to an edge or bar at one orientation (Hubel & Wiesel, Nobel Prize 1981).
Vision.Kernels.Tip: The convolution kernels the model filters the image with. Teal = excitatory, pink = inhibitory region.
Vision.Load.Tip: Load a photograph (PNG, JPG, BMP). It is converted to greyscale and resized to a 96×96 photoreceptor “retina”.
Vision.LoadFailed: The image could not be loaded. Try another PNG or JPG file.
Vision.Paint.Tip: When on, draw on panel 1 with the mouse (left button: draw, right button: erase).
Vision.PaintWhite.Tip: Brush colour. The right mouse button always paints the opposite colour.
Vision.Pathway: Retina (photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells) → optic nerve → thalamus (LGN) → primary visual cortex (V1). The model follows this chain: DoG filtering in the retina, Gabor energy in V1.
Vision.Preset.None.Tip: Surround switched off: the illusions vanish, the image is merely blurred.
Vision.Preset.Strong.Tip: Balanced centre–surround: maximal edge enhancement and illusions.
Vision.Preset.Wide.Tip: Fields twice as large, as in the visual periphery: coarser resolution.
Vision.Profile.Tip: Along the selected row (dashed yellow line): input brightness (grey) and the centre–surround response (teal). The overshoot at each step explains the Mach bands.
Vision.Receptive.Tip: Parameters of the ganglion cells' centre–surround (difference of Gaussians, DoG) and the V1 cells' Gabor receptive fields.
Vision.SpikeRate: {0} Hz per cell on average · {1} spikes this frame
Vision.Stage.Contrast.Tip: The signed DoG response (teal = positive, pink = negative). Uniform regions vanish and only changes – edges – remain: the retina already compresses!
Vision.Stage.Input.Tip: The image falling on the retina: cones and rods measure light intensity. Click to move the profile line; in drawing mode you can paint on it.
Vision.Stage.Off.Tip: They fire when the centre is darker than the surround. Together the ON and OFF channels encode contrast in both directions.
Vision.Stage.On.Tip: They fire when the centre of the receptive field is brighter than its surround. Bright spots and the light side of edges activate them.
Vision.Stage.Spikes.Tip: This is how the image reaches the brain: as spike trains along ~1 million optic-nerve fibres. Green = ON, magenta = OFF spikes (Poisson process, shown at quarter speed).
Vision.Stage.V1.Tip: Complex cells of the primary visual cortex: for each pixel the colour of the most strongly responding orientation (see legend); brightness is selectivity.
Vision.Stimulus.Tip: Pick a built-in stimulus – including classic optical illusions – draw your own or load a photograph.
Vision.Surround.Tip: Radius of the inhibitory surround (always larger than the centre).
Vision.Wavelength.Tip: Spatial period of the Gabor filters: the bar width / spatial frequency preferred by the V1 cells.
